newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam pledges export drive to tackle trade gap.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam pledges export drive to tackle trade gap.

text.p: Vietnam's new finance minister on Monday promised an export drive to tackle a ballooning trade deficit and said saddling the country with fresh borrowings from abroad was no quick-fix solution.
Nguyen Sinh Hung, an economy expert who was promoted from deputy minister of finance in a cabinet reshuffle last week, said the trade gap was a problem, but not yet a grave one.
"Currently it's not that serious," he told reporters during a break in National Assembly proceedings. "But if this trend is sustained that will be dangerous."
The Trade Ministry last week reported a near-record trade deficit of $3.49 billion for the first 10 months of this year and predicted that the gap was set to widen even further.
It said the full-year deficit was expected to be $4 billion, up sharply from $2.3 billion in 1995 and its highest-ever level.
Communist Vietnam's reform-led economic boom and rapidly increasing income levels have brought an unprecedented boom in imports.
The government says much of its imports are capital goods which will ultimately generate production and exports.

But it has expressed concern about rapid growth in imports of consumer goods and some officials have suggested implementing a drive to substitute or even curb imports. That has heightened concern about Hanoi's commitment to trade liberalisation.
Hung said that a newly amended foreign investment law, which includes tax breaks for export-oriented enterprises, was one of many steps being taken to encourage the sale of goods abroad.
He said that while the private sector was still too small to export much, the government was keen to establish a level playing field for both private firms and the sprawling state sector.
The finance minister also said the government would move to control "unecessary" imports and fight against smuggling.
Smuggling -- estimated at around $1.9 billion last year -- is a major, but hidden, drain on Vietnam's trade account particularly as most of the goods are consumer products.
Hung said Vietnam, which is still negotiating with foreign commercial creditors on repaying nearly $1 billion of debt, was not seeking new foreign loans to fill immediate finance gaps.
"We understand that this (foreign borrowing) will be a channel for Vietnam to mobilise money, but we will do it only when we have adequate conditions," he said.
"We don't think this would be a good idea. It is not a good way to solve budget problems by borrowing more."
The World Bank has been advising Hanoi to hold back from making a debut international bond issue until it has restructured its commercial debt obligations.
Hung also moved to scotch speculation that Vietnam was planning a devaluation of the local currency, the dong, to redress its trade imbalance.
"The Vietnamese government or the (central) bank have never mentioned the possibility of devaluing the...currency," he said. "That's why I don't think it's an issue to be discussed."
